summary.text: The **RAAS**: angiotensinogen → (renin) → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone; aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone antagonists each block one step.

**ACE inhibitors/ARBs** are first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure; a creatinine rise **up to ~30%** is expected; check K⁺/creatinine in 1–2 weeks; **never in pregnancy**.

chunks.text: **One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.
ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.
**Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.
**ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.
**Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**
Cough is bradykinin-mediated, not allergic. Angioedema is rare but can be life-threatening: stop the drug.

An initial rise in serum creatinine of up to ~30% after starting therapy is expected and acceptable — reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not drug-induced kidney injury; a larger rise warrants evaluation for renal artery stenosis.

Students frequently get the creatinine point wrong: many want to stop the ACE inhibitor at the first rise. It is a predictable hemodynamic effect, not toxicity — the mechanism and the "side effect" are two faces of the same action.
**Contraindicated in pregnancy — fetal renal toxicity; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant.** ARBs share the same pregnancy contraindication and hyperkalemia risk as ACE inhibitors.
Aliskiren: generally not combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB due to additive hyperkalemia/hypotension risk with no added benefit — never in diabetes.

Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. NSAIDs blunt antihypertensives and raise AKI risk with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.
Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics rises with drugs that cut renin or angiotensin II: β blockers, NSAIDs, aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.
Enalapril’s ACE-inhibition half-life is about 4 hours, yet once-daily dosing works: concentrations stay far above the C50, so ACE stays inhibited.
**Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

chunks.text: Why does creatinine rise on an ACE inhibitor? The drug lowers glomerular pressure on purpose — that same drop protects the kidney from proteinuria.
Thirty is fine, more is a sign: up to ~30% creatinine rise → continue; more → look for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
**RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.
Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.
Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.
Hydralazine: reflex tachycardia and fluid retention — must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic.
Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.
Atenolol accumulates in renal impairment (reduce dose when CrCl is below 35 mL/min); beta-blockers: do not stop abruptly.
Diltiazem or verapamil with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia and AV block; dihydropyridines pair with beta-blockers without that conduction risk.
Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels. Rifampin and carbamazepine lower CCB levels; grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.
**Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

"Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

Case: CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min), still hypertensive despite lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. **What is the most likely contributor to inadequate control, and what change would you suggest first?**

**At this GFR, hydrochlorothiazide has largely lost its natriuretic efficacy (Session 1). Switching to a loop diuretic such as furosemide or torsemide is usually the most effective next step before adding an entirely new drug class.**
This case is a direct callback to the Session 1 "Choosing a Diuretic for Advancing CKD" case — point out the parallel if you remember it.

**Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.
Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).

**Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**
CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.
**Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**
**Adverse effects: peripheral edema and reflex tachycardia (dihydropyridines); bradycardia, AV block, and constipation (non-dihydropyridines, especially verapamil).**
**Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

**Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.
Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.
The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

Why are nitrates + sildenafil deadly? Nitrates make cGMP; sildenafil stops its breakdown — cGMP piles up and blood pressure collapses.

**Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

**1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.
**Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.
**A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.
**Recall Q1–2:** loops collapse the lumen-positive potential (↑ Ca²⁺ excretion), thiazides increase distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; at eGFR 22 switch the thiazide to a loop.
**Recall Q3–4:** a creatinine rise up to ~30% on an ACE inhibitor is expected — continue with monitoring; ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
**Recall Q5:** the triple whammy is three independent reductions in filtration pressure combining additively to synergistically, precipitating AKI.

**Recall Q6:** CCBs treat hypertension via arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload/systemic vascular resistance) and angina via the same mechanism (reducing afterload and myocardial oxygen demand) — one drug class, one mechanism, two indications.
Reflexively stopping an ACE inhibitor for a ≤30% creatinine rise is the classic trap.
Adding a new drug class when the real problem is a thiazide at low GFR.

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 2
2.notes:
Briefly recap Session 1 before diving in: diuretic pharmacology by nephron site, and the hyperkalemia-with-ACEi/ARB preview from the closing case. Today extends that same cardiorenal thread through RAAS-blocking antihypertensives, other antihypertensive classes, and the vasodilator/angina overlap, closing with a cumulative recall quiz spanning both sessions.

Instructor script:

Today we follow one pathway, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, then see where it intersects with angina drugs and with the most preventable cause of AKI, the triple whammy.

3.notes: Section transition. Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway that the drugs in this section act on.

4.title: The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System: Where Antihypertensives Act
4.notes:
This is the conceptual spine for the entire session — every drug class in Section 4 and much of Section 5 maps onto this single pathway. Walk it step by step before naming any individual drugs, so students see the cascade logic first.

Instructor script:

Walk the cascade before naming drugs: angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.

5.title: ACE Inhibitors
5.notes:
The "up to 30% creatinine rise is expected" point is one students frequently get wrong on exams and in practice — many will want to stop the ACE inhibitor at the first sign of a rising creatinine. Be explicit that this is a predictable hemodynamic effect, not toxicity.

Instructor script:

Block ACE. Cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia; pregnancy contraindication; creatinine rise up to about 30% is expected.

6.title: ACE Inhibitors: Bradykinin, Cough and Angioedema
6.notes:
Explain that bradykinin accumulation is the mechanism of ACE-inhibitor cough; switch to an ARB if cough is troublesome.

Instructor script:

ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it raises bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema. ARBs spare bradykinin.

7.title: ARBs and Direct Renin Inhibitors
7.notes:
Aliskiren is included mainly for conceptual completeness on Figure 8 — keep this brief and emphasize that ACE inhibitors and ARBs are the clinically dominant classes, while flagging the combination-therapy caution as a safety point worth remembering.

Instructor script:

Losartan and valsartan block AT1. Aliskiren is limited and never combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB in diabetes.

8.title: RAAS Blockers in Chronic Kidney Disease
8.notes:
This slide is the clinical payoff of Figure 8 and the pregnancy/creatinine points from the ACE inhibitor slide — make the connection explicit: the drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.

Instructor script:

Efferent arteriole dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.

9.title: Efferent Arteriole Dilation: Why Creatinine Rises
9.notes:
Frame the creatinine rise as a predictable hemodynamic effect; reinforce sick-day rules.

Instructor script:

The benefit and the creatinine rise are the same action. Monitor potassium and creatinine in 1-2 weeks; use sick-day rules.

10.title: Interpreting a Creatinine Rise After Starting Lisinopril
10.notes:
This case directly tests whether the renoprotective-mechanism slide landed — a student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed the point that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

Instructor script:

1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL is about 27%; continue and monitor.

11.notes: Section transition. Other major antihypertensive classes come next: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.

12.title: Other Major Antihypertensive Classes
12.notes:
This four-card slide is a deliberate, brief recap — calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework. The point here is classification, not exhaustive detail.

Instructor script:

CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.

13.title: Calcium Channel Blockers and Beta-Blockers: Different Targets
13.notes:
Contrast vascular dilation with cardiac slowing; flag the diltiazem or verapamil plus beta-blocker combination.

Instructor script:

Dihydropyridines dilate arterioles; non-dihydropyridines and beta-blockers slow heart rate and contractility. Avoid diltiazem or verapamil with a beta-blocker.

14.title: Antihypertensive Classes: BP-Lowering Efficacy vs. Renoprotection in CKD
14.notes:
Use this figure to directly answer "if all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD?" — the answer is the renoprotective gap shown here, not a difference in BP control.

Instructor script:

Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection.

15.title: Resistant Hypertension in CKD
15.notes:
This slide ties Session 1 and Session 2 together directly — "resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class.

Instructor script:

Check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

16.title: Central Agents and Hydralazine: When Others Are Not Enough
16.notes:
Contrast central sympatholytics with direct vasodilators, and stress the beta-blocker and diuretic pairing for hydralazine.

Instructor script:

Clonidine and methyldopa reduce sympathetic outflow; hydralazine dilates arterioles with reflex tachycardia. Methyldopa in pregnancy; clonidine rebound.

17.title: Resistant Hypertension — Where to Look First
17.notes:
This case is a direct callback to the Session 1 "Choosing a Diuretic for Advancing CKD" case — point out the parallel explicitly if students remember it.

Instructor script:

Case cue: pause and ask the class where to look first before revealing the answer.

18.notes: Section transition. This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.

19.title: Nitrates
19.notes:
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — always worth a specific, memorable callout since it is a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question.

Instructor script:

Venodilation, tolerance, nitrate-free interval; PDE5 inhibitor contraindication.

20.title: Nitrates: NO, cGMP and Venodilation
20.notes:
Walk through the NO to cGMP pathway, then stress PDE5 inhibitor co-prescription and the nitrate-free interval.

Instructor script:

Nitric oxide, guanylate cyclase, cGMP, relaxation; sildenafil blocks cGMP breakdown.

21.title: Angina Pathophysiology: Where Nitrates and Calcium Channel Blockers Act
21.notes:
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — have students sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto this diagram from memory before revealing the labels.

Instructor script:

Have students sort drugs by supply or demand effect.

22.title: Calcium Channel Blockers for Angina
22.notes:
This slide is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5, they are the same drugs doing double duty.

Instructor script:

Same class and mechanism treats hypertension and angina.

23.title: The "Triple Whammy": A Classic Preventable Cause of AKI
23.notes:
This is the capstone cardiorenal-interaction figure for the whole unit — it combines Session 1's diuretic content, this session's RAAS-blocker content, and a drug class (NSAIDs) students will encounter constantly in practice. Make the point explicit: this is an extremely common, often missed, and entirely preventable cause of AKI.

Instructor script:

NSAID plus ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.

24.title: Triple Whammy: Three Hits on Glomerular Pressure
24.notes:
Explain how each of the three drugs lowers glomerular filtration pressure, and ask students to name the OTC NSAIDs patients commonly take.

Instructor script:

Afferent constriction, efferent dilation, volume depletion.

25.title: The Cardiorenal-Hypertension Relationship
25.notes:
Direct students to Figure 18 (the next slide) for the visual version of this same bidirectional relationship — this slide states it in words first.

Instructor script:

Hypertension drives CKD and CKD drives hypertension.

26.title: The Cardiorenal-Hypertension Cycle
26.notes:
This figure is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it explicitly back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Instructor script:

RAAS blockade interrupts both directions.

27.title: Recognizing the Triple Whammy
27.notes:
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and a strong closing vignette for the section — it also reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling), since the preventable element here is entirely about what the patient was or wasn't told about OTC NSAID use.

Instructor script:

Case cue: pause and ask the class to spot the triple whammy before revealing the answer.

28.title: Drug Names Reveal the Class: Cardiorenal Agents
28.notes:
Walk the stems row by row and ask students to predict the class from the suffix before revealing it.

Instructor script:

-pril, -sartan, -kiren, -dipine, -olol, -onidine, -afil.

29.notes: Section transition. Integration: we now put the drug classes together.

30.title: Which Approach Would You Choose?
30.notes:
Have students work in pairs: for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

Instructor script:

Work in pairs: first-line approach and the biggest safety check for each patient.

U5-R8.question: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in proteinuric CKD, beyond their blood-pressure-lowering effect?

U5-R9.question: An expected creatinine rise of up to roughly what percentage after starting an ACE inhibitor is considered acceptable, and what does a larger rise suggest?

U5-R10.question: Compare dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers: which one is also used for hypertension via the same mechanism it uses for angina?

U5-R11.question: Describe the mechanism of nitrates in angina and state their absolute contraindication.

U5-R12.question: Explain the "triple whammy" — which three drug classes are involved, and what does each one independently do to glomerular filtration pressure?

U5-S.question:
An older adult with hypertension, managed on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, develops a knee injury and starts taking an over-the-counter NSAID regularly for pain relief. One week later, the patient presents with lethargy and is found to have an acute rise in creatinine. Separately, this same patient's hypertension has crept up over recent visits, and their eGFR has fallen to 25 mL/min.
What is the most likely explanation for the acute creatinine rise, and what pharmacologic principle explains why these three particular drug classes are dangerous together?
Given the patient's advancing CKD (eGFR 25), is hydrochlorothiazide still an appropriate choice for their blood pressure, independent of the NSAID issue? What would you change, and why?
How would you counsel this patient to prevent this combination from recurring, given that the triggering drug was available over the counter?
U5-S.answer: This is a classic "triple whammy" — the NSAID, the ACE inhibitor, and the diuretic each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure by a distinct mechanism, and together the effect is additive to synergistic, precipitating AKI. Separately, at eGFR 25, hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is the more effective choice for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue. Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

children.name: Class
facts: **One pathway, four drug classes, and the preferred therapy for hypertension in CKD.** Today we follow the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, the pathway these drugs act on.

**Figure 8. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angiotensinogen is converted to angiotensin I by renin, then to angiotensin II by ACE; angiotensin II drives both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.**
**Direct renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and aldosterone antagonists each block a different point in this cascade.**
This is the conceptual spine for the session: walk the cascade before naming drugs — angiotensinogen, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, vasoconstriction and aldosterone.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: ACE inhibitors: captopril, lisinopril, enalapril — "-pril" suffix across the class. ARBs: losartan, valsartan — "-sartan" suffix. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing both vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (Figure 8).**

ACE also breaks down bradykinin: ACE inhibitor blocks ACE → less angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) → less bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin accumulates → cough or angioedema → switch to an ARB for cough.
ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly, rather than preventing angiotensin II formation. Aliskiren blocks the rate-limiting first step of the entire cascade.

Renoprotection: by reducing angiotensin II, these drugs preferentially dilate the efferent (outflow) arteriole of the glomerulus, lowering intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria — a direct, structural renoprotective effect beyond systemic BP control.

Chain (Figure 10): angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that signal → efferent arteriole dilates; intraglomerular pressure falls → proteinuria falls; creatinine rises up to ~30%.

children.name: Indications
facts: **ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line antihypertensive therapy in CKD, especially with proteinuria — not simply because they lower blood pressure.**
ARBs: no bradykinin-related cough — preferred alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable. ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
Aliskiren: limited clinical use; useful mainly as a teaching example of where a drug could act upstream of ACE — included for conceptual completeness on Figure 8.
The drug class students might expect to avoid in kidney disease is actually the preferred therapy, precisely because of how it works at the glomerulus.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: dry cough (bradykinin accumulation — the single most common reason for switching to an ARB), angioedema (rare but potentially life-threatening), and hyperkalemia.**
Cough is bradykinin-mediated, not allergic. Angioedema is rare but can be life-threatening: stop the drug.

An initial rise in serum creatinine of up to ~30% after starting therapy is expected and acceptable — reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not drug-induced kidney injury; a larger rise warrants evaluation for renal artery stenosis.

Students frequently get the creatinine point wrong: many want to stop the ACE inhibitor at the first rise. It is a predictable hemodynamic effect, not toxicity — the mechanism and the "side effect" are two faces of the same action.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Contraindicated in pregnancy — fetal renal toxicity; avoid in women who are or may become pregnant.** ARBs share the same pregnancy contraindication and hyperkalemia risk as ACE inhibitors.
Aliskiren: generally not combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB due to additive hyperkalemia/hypotension risk with no added benefit — never in diabetes.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics and trimethoprim: hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. NSAIDs blunt antihypertensives and raise AKI risk with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic.
Hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics rises with drugs that cut renin or angiotensin II: β blockers, NSAIDs, aliskiren, ACE inhibitors, ARBs.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Enalapril’s ACE-inhibition half-life is about 4 hours, yet once-daily dosing works: concentrations stay far above the C50, so ACE stays inhibited.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks of starting or up-titrating therapy, and periodically thereafter.**
**Hold or use with caution during acute illness causing volume depletion ("sick day rules") — combined with reduced renal perfusion, RAAS blockade can precipitate acute kidney injury.**

Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration. An early creatinine rise is expected and hemodynamic, not nephrotoxicity; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a patient with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on lisinopril; two weeks later serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. **Is this an indication to stop the ACE inhibitor?**
**A rise of roughly 27% is within the expected range for ACE inhibitor initiation, reflecting reduced intraglomerular pressure from efferent arteriolar dilation — not drug toxicity.**
**Therapy should generally continue with ongoing monitoring; a rise beyond approximately 30%, or a much sharper increase, should prompt evaluation for renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.**
A student who reflexively says "stop the drug" has missed that this creatinine rise is expected and even reflects the mechanism working as intended.

children.name: Class
facts: **RAAS blockers are first-line — but rarely the whole story.** Other major classes: CCBs, beta-blockers, diuretics, central agents and direct vasodilators.
This four-card slide is a brief classification recap — CCBs and beta-blockers get fuller treatment later this session (angina) and in cardiovascular coursework.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Calcium channel blockers: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) and non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil). Beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol. Central α2 agonists: clonidine, methyldopa. Direct arteriolar vasodilator: hydralazine.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine): arteriolar dilation. Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil): also ↓ HR/contractility.
Beta-blockers: ↓ heart rate, ↓ contractility, ↓ renin release.
Chain (Figure 11): dihydropyridine arteriolar dilation → afterload falls; blood pressure lowers. Non-DHP CCB or beta-blocker: heart rate and contractility fall → renin release falls.
Clonidine or methyldopa stimulates central α2 receptors → sympathetic outflow falls, so BP falls. Hydralazine dilates arterioles directly → reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.

children.name: Indications
facts: Beta-blockers: not generally first-line for uncomplicated HTN, but compelling indications include concurrent CAD/heart failure/arrhythmia.

If all these classes lower blood pressure similarly, why are RAAS blockers preferred in CKD? Similar BP lowering; ACE inhibitors and ARBs add renoprotection — the renoprotective gap in Figure 12, not a difference in BP control.
Thiazide / loop diuretics (covered in depth in Session 1): thiazides first-line with preserved renal function; loops preferred as GFR falls.
Central agents (clonidine, methyldopa) and hydralazine: reserved for resistant hypertension or specific situations (e.g., methyldopa in pregnancy).
Diuretics enhance the efficacy of many agents, particularly ACE inhibitors; hydralazine and minoxidil need a diuretic because they cause salt and water retention.
Spironolactone may be the most effective single agent for drug-resistant hypertension.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect.
Hydralazine: reflex tachycardia and fluid retention — must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic.
Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Atenolol accumulates in renal impairment (reduce dose when CrCl is below 35 mL/min); beta-blockers: do not stop abruptly.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Diltiazem or verapamil with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia and AV block; dihydropyridines pair with beta-blockers without that conduction risk.
Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels. Rifampin and carbamazepine lower CCB levels; grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Resistant hypertension (BP above goal despite three or more antihypertensive classes, including a diuretic) is common in CKD, often driven by volume overload.**
First step: confirm diuretic therapy is adequate — a thiazide may simply no longer be effective at the patient’s current GFR (Session 1’s loop-vs-thiazide cutoff).
Switching from a thiazide to a loop diuretic, or increasing loop diuretic dosing, is often the most effective single change in advanced CKD.
**Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) can be added for resistant hypertension, but require close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially on top of an ACE inhibitor or ARB.**

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: "Resistant hypertension in CKD" is often really a diuretic-selection problem, not a need for an entirely new drug class — check diuretic adequacy first; thiazide to loop switch; add spironolactone with close monitoring.

Case: CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min), still hypertensive despite lisinopril, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide. **What is the most likely contributor to inadequate control, and what change would you suggest first?**

**At this GFR, hydrochlorothiazide has largely lost its natriuretic efficacy (Session 1). Switching to a loop diuretic such as furosemide or torsemide is usually the most effective next step before adding an entirely new drug class.**
This case is a direct callback to the Session 1 "Choosing a Diuretic for Advancing CKD" case — point out the parallel if you remember it.

tree.name: Part 3 · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy

children.name: Class
facts: **Where cardiovascular and renal pharmacology converge — and where that convergence can go wrong.** This section covers vasodilators and angina, then the cardiorenal overlap.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): angina results when myocardial oxygen demand exceeds supply; nitrates reduce preload, dihydropyridine CCBs reduce afterload,**
**non-dihydropyridine CCBs also reduce heart rate/contractility and increase coronary flow, and beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility.**
This figure organizes every antianginal drug class by exactly which side of the supply/demand equation it affects — sort nitrates, each CCB subtype, and beta-blockers onto it from memory.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Nitroglycerin (sublingual for acute angina; IV/patch for sustained use), isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate (oral, longer-acting).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: release nitric oxide, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP, producing smooth muscle relaxation — predominantly venodilation at usual doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.**
Chain (Figure 14): nitrate donates nitric oxide (NO) → NO activates guanylate cyclase, so cGMP rises → cGMP relaxes smooth muscle: venodilation → preload and oxygen demand fall.
**Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) — predominantly arteriolar dilation, reducing afterload; the same mechanism used for hypertension (Section 5).**

**Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem, verapamil) — also reduce heart rate and contractility and increase coronary blood flow; avoid combining with beta-blockers due to additive bradycardia/AV block risk.**

children.name: Indications
facts: CCBs are the clearest example in the unit of the same drug class, same mechanism, treating two different conditions (hypertension and angina).

This is the deliberate cardiovascular-renal "overlap" moment the lecture title promises — calcium channel blockers are not a separate topic from the antihypertensive content in Section 5; they are the same drugs doing double duty.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.**
**Adverse effects: peripheral edema and reflex tachycardia (dihydropyridines); bradycardia, AV block, and constipation (non-dihydropyridines, especially verapamil).**

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Absolute contraindication: concurrent use with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and similar) — the combination can cause life-threatening hypotension.**
PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil block cGMP breakdown, causing severe hypotension with nitrates.
The PDE5-inhibitor interaction is one of the highest-stakes medication-safety points in this whole unit — a real-world, repeatedly tested safety question worth a memorable callout.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Figure 16. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): an NSAID (afferent arteriolar constriction), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent arteriolar dilation), and a diuretic (volume depletion) each independently reduce glomerular filtration pressure —**
**combined, the effect on kidney perfusion is additive to synergistic, substantially raising acute kidney injury risk.** An extremely common, often missed, entirely preventable cause of AKI.
Three hits (Figure 17): NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole → ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent arteriole → diuretic causes volume depletion → filtration pressure collapses: AKI.
NSAIDs blunt loop and thiazide action by reducing renal prostaglandins — significant in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure — a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.
Prevention: counsel patients about over-the-counter NSAIDs — ask which OTC NSAIDs they commonly take.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The triple whammy is the capstone cardiorenal interaction: Session 1’s diuretics + this session’s RAAS blockers + NSAIDs students will meet constantly in practice.
Hypertension → CKD: uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular capillary injury and nephrosclerosis over time — a leading cause of CKD progression, alongside diabetes.
CKD → hypertension: reduced renal function causes volume overload and RAAS activation, which worsens and complicates blood pressure control, often requiring multiple drug classes.

**Figure 18. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hypertension and chronic kidney disease drive one another in a self-reinforcing cycle — uncontrolled blood pressure causes glomerular injury and CKD progression,**
**while CKD causes volume overload and RAAS activation that worsens hypertension.**
Figure 18 is the conceptual closer for the whole unit — tie it back to Figure 8: RAAS blockade is effective precisely because it intervenes in both directions of this cycle at once.

Case: an older adult on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide starts a regular OTC NSAID for a knee injury; one week later, lethargy and an acute rise in creatinine. **What is the most likely explanation, and how could this have been prevented?**

**This is a classic "triple whammy" presentation (Figure 16) — the NSAID, ACE inhibitor, and diuretic each independently reduced glomerular filtration pressure, and together precipitated acute kidney injury.**
**Prevention requires counseling patients on RAAS blockers and diuretics to avoid regular NSAID use and to seek guidance before starting one, even an over-the-counter product.**
This case is the direct clinical application of Figure 16 and reinforces IO5.6 (patient counseling): the preventable element is entirely what the patient was or wasn’t told about OTC NSAID use.

Same patient, eGFR now 25: hydrochlorothiazide has likely lost much of its efficacy — switching to a loop diuretic (furosemide, torsemide) is more effective for blood pressure regardless of the NSAID issue.
Counsel the patient to avoid regular OTC NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before starting any new OTC product, given the RAAS blocker + diuretic combination already in place.

tree.name: Part 4 · Putting It All Together: Renal Toolkit

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Applying the whole Renal pharmacology toolkit.** Integration: put the drug classes together — for each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing or counseling.

children.name: How it works
facts: **1.** Diuretic classes (Session 1) and RAAS-blocking antihypertensives both map onto specific, drug-targetable points in renal physiology — the nephron (Figure 1) and the RAAS cascade (Figure 8), respectively.
**2.** ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred first-line therapy for hypertension in CKD because of their renoprotective efferent-arteriolar mechanism, not just their blood-pressure-lowering effect.
**3.** Calcium channel blockers exemplify the cardiovascular-renal overlap directly — the same drug class, same mechanism, treats both hypertension and angina.
**4.** The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a classic, common, and preventable cause of acute kidney injury that draws on content from both sessions at once.
**5.** Hypertension and chronic kidney disease exist in a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle (Figure 18) — which is exactly why managing one well so often means managing the other.
All three threads center on glomerular filtration pressure.

Connecting back to earlier units: drug-metabolism/dosing concepts (Unit 1) and the biologic-mechanism callbacks from Units 2–4 all reinforce that pharmacology is cumulative — the cardiorenal interface is where several organ-system units visibly intersect.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: **Patient A — advancing CKD, hypertension no longer controlled on a thiazide:** switch to a loop diuretic; check potassium and volume status.
**Patient B — proteinuric CKD, needs first-line antihypertensive therapy:** ACE inhibitor or ARB; check potassium and creatinine in 1–2 weeks and pregnancy potential.
**Patient C — on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, about to start a daily OTC NSAID:** counsel against regular NSAID use — triple whammy AKI risk.

**Patient D — stable angina, already on a beta-blocker, needs additional symptom control:** add a dihydropyridine CCB or a long-acting nitrate; avoid diltiazem/verapamil (AV block) and PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: **A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.
**Recall Q1–2:** loops collapse the lumen-positive potential (↑ Ca²⁺ excretion), thiazides increase distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; at eGFR 22 switch the thiazide to a loop.
**Recall Q3–4:** a creatinine rise up to ~30% on an ACE inhibitor is expected — continue with monitoring; ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
**Recall Q5:** the triple whammy is three independent reductions in filtration pressure combining additively to synergistically, precipitating AKI.

**Recall Q6:** CCBs treat hypertension via arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload/systemic vascular resistance) and angina via the same mechanism (reducing afterload and myocardial oxygen demand) — one drug class, one mechanism, two indications.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Reflexively stopping an ACE inhibitor for a ≤30% creatinine rise is the classic trap.
Adding a new drug class when the real problem is a thiazide at low GFR.

hy: ACEi/ARB first-line in proteinuric CKD: efferent dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.
Creatinine rise up to ~30% is expected; check K⁺ and creatinine in 1–2 weeks; sick-day rules; never in pregnancy.
Non-DHP CCB + beta-blocker → bradycardia/AV block; DHP + beta-blocker is fine.
Resistant HTN in CKD: fix the diuretic first (thiazide → loop), then spironolactone with K⁺ monitoring.

brief.part: Part 3 · Nitrates, Angina & the Triple Whammy
hy: Nitrates: NO → cGMP → venodilation, ↓ preload; nitrate-free interval; never with PDE5 inhibitors.
Triple whammy: NSAID (afferent) + ACEi/ARB (efferent) + diuretic (volume) → AKI; counsel on OTC NSAIDs.
